entities.summary:
The Franciscans emerged in the early 13th century, founded by Saint Francis of Assisi (1181-1226) in Italy, and represent a pivotal movement within the Catholic Church that emphasized poverty, humility, and the love of nature. Their foundation around 1209 marked a significant shift in religious life, promoting a return to the simple teachings of Christ and advocating for the marginalized. The Franciscans quickly spread throughout Europe, establishing communities and influencing religious practices, ultimately becoming a major force in medieval spirituality and education.

The Order of Friars Minor, the first of the three orders established by Francis, was formally recognized by Pope Innocent III in 1209. Following this, the Order of Saint Clare, dedicated to women, was founded in 1212, while the Third Order was established in 1221 to allow laypeople to live out Franciscan ideals. These orders played crucial roles in the development of mendicant orders, which became integral to the fabric of medieval society, promoting social justice and education, and forming the basis for modern Catholic social teaching.

The legacy of the Franciscans is profound, influencing subsequent religious movements and contributing to the Catholic Reformation. Their commitment to social justice and care for creation resonates today, with organizations worldwide continuing their mission. The Franciscans helped shape a more compassionate and accessible Church, impacting the way Christianity engages with social issues, poverty, and the environment.

Reflecting on their enduring influence, Saint Francis's profound statement, 'Preach the Gospel at all times; when necessary, use words,' encapsulates the essence of Franciscan spirituality and its call to live out faith through action, inspiring countless individuals and movements throughout history.
